list-item.p: PET mTMTV showed prognostic impact in NDMM.
Baseline PET was complementary to R-ISS to stratify prognosis.

abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: This study aimed to assess the prognostic value of medullary total metabolic tumor volume (mTMTV) derived from fluorodeoxyglucose–positron emission tomography/computed tomography ([18F]FDG-PET/CT) compared with conventional PET-derived features and biological/chromosomal abnormalities in patients with newly diagnosed multiple myeloma (NDMM) treated with daratumumab for induction/consolidation and/or maintenance and enrolled in CASSIOPET, a companion study of CASSIOPEIA, with long-term follow-up. Automated bone/liver CT–based segmentation were applied to the baseline [18F]FDG-PET images, with mTMTV being defined using the median liver background as the cut-off, including focal lesions and diffuse bone marrow (BM) involvement. Both univariate/multivariate Cox and machine learning (ML)–based survival models were performed. A total of 195 patients were included, 81% of them PET-positive. Multivariate analysis demonstrated independent prognostic value of mTMTV for progression-free survival (PFS) (P < .001) and overall survival (OS) (P < .001), complementary to Revised International Staging System (R-ISS) (P = .008 and P < .001, respectively). The ML model confirmed these findings, achieving concordance index of 0.609 and 0.659 and identifying mTMTV as the most informative feature for PFS and OS. Adding R-ISS, BM maximum standardized uptake value (SUVmax) and anemia to mTMTV accounted for >60% of the ML model explanation for PFS and adding R-ISS, the number of focal lesions and BM SUVmax for >60% of the model for OS. Combining R-ISS and mTMTV enabled the creation of 2 new-risk subgroups. In conclusion, this prospective study demonstrated the prognostic relevance of [18F]FDG-PET/CT–based parameters in the initial workup of patients with NDMM in the era of anti-CD38–based therapy. mTMTV was found to have strong independent prognostic value, complementary to R-ISS and refining risk stratification. This trial was registered at www.clinicaltrials.gov as #NCT02541383.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Multiple myeloma (MM) is a heterogeneous disease characterized by patchy infiltration of the bone marrow (BM) by clonal plasma cells. Despite significant therapeutic advances over the past decade leading to a substantial increase in patient survival, some patients with newly diagnosed MM (NDMM) still experience an early relapse after the initiation of first-line therapy. Therefore, identifying high-risk biomarkers at the initial workup is crucial for predicting survival and potentially adapting therapy. According to the latest International Myeloma Society/International Myeloma Working Group consensus recommendations,1 high-risk MM are defined solely by chromosomal abnormalities and biological data, not including functional imaging biomarkers.

Whole-body [18F]-fluorodeoxyglucose-positron emission tomography coupled with computed tomography ([18F]FDG-PET/CT) is one of the recommended imaging techniques for the initial workup of patients with NDMM,2 for detecting medullary and extramedullary disease (EMD), and for predicting outcomes.3 Indeed, all large prospective studies conducted in transplant-eligible patients with NDMM over the past 15 years have demonstrated that several [18F]FDG-PET-derived biomarkers adversely affect progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS). These biomarkers include a high number of bone focal lesions (FLs), the maximum standardized uptake value (SUVmax) of FLs or large FL, the presence of EMD,4, 5, 6, 7 and, more recently, [18F]FDG-PET positivity,8 a high BM SUVmax9,10 or the presence of FLs with contiguous soft tissue extension, known as paramedullary disease (PMD).11

However, in most cases, these conventional PET-based prognostic biomarkers were determined using data from patients treated with currently less used therapies. Thus, they may no longer accurately predict prognosis in the new era of quadruplet therapies. Therefore, risk stratification using these conventional PET biomarkers needs to be updated to reflect current treatment standards. Furthermore, new PET metrics, such as total metabolic tumor volume12 (TMTV) may help to improve the discriminative value of [18F]FDG-PET related to prognostic factors. This biomarker assesses tumor burden in [18F]FDG-avid disease. Previous studies have shown the potential adverse prognostic value of a high baseline TMTV based solely on the delineation of FLs for PFS and OS.13, 14, 15, 16 Recently, a more comprehensive medullary TMTV (mTMTV), which includes both diffuse BM involvement (BMI) and [18F]FDG-avid FLs (with uptake related to the liver) has been proposed by Sachpekidis et al17 to alleviate the limited inter-reader reproducibility in scan interpretation due to different patterns of BMI and to assess its prognostic value.

The primary objective of CASSIOPET, a companion study of CASSIOPEIA, was to evaluate the prognostic value for premaintenance [18F]FDG-PET/CT response based on the standardized Deauville score on PFS and OS in addition to BM minimal residual disease detection.18 A preliminary analysis of CASSIOPET assessed the prognostic value of conventional features derived from [18F]FDG-PET at baseline, that is, at the time of the first randomization, for PFS, using a short-term median follow-up period of 2 years. This analysis confirmed the adverse prognostic impact of various PET parameters, including [18F]FDG global positivity and the presence of EMD or PMD.11

The present study aimed to assess the additional prognostic value of [18F]FDG-PET/CT-derived mTMTV for PFS and OS compared to conventional PET biomarkers and typical biological/chromosomal abnormalities in the initial workup of patients with NDMM from the CASSIOPET study with long-term follow-up.

sec.title: Patients
sec.p: This study considered patients enrolled in the 2-phase CASSIOPEIA trial, the design of which, along with the eligibility criteria, has been previously published.19 Patients from the CASSIOPEIA trial were enrolled in the CASSIOPET ancillary study if they had undergone a [18F]FDG-PET/CT scan within 6 weeks of the first randomization. Patients were excluded if they were unable to access a [18F]FDG-PET/CT scanner or remain motionless for the duration of the scan, had uncontrolled diabetes, or had received steroids within 12 hours prior to the scan. Figure 1 shows the flowchart of patients included in this study. Only the patients from the CASSIOPET study who received daratumumab (DARA) treatment at the first and/or second randomization were considered, as significantly improved PFS was demonstrated with DARA, bortezomib, thalidomide, and dexamethasone vs bortezomib, thalidomide, and dexamethasone as induction, consolidation and maintenance in patients with autologous stem-cell transplant-eligible NDMM in the different CASSIOPEIA publications.19, 20, 21 In the CASSIOPEIA study, high cytogenetic risk was defined as the presence of t(4;14) (≥30% abnormal cells) or del(17p) (≥50% abnormal cells) chromosomal abnormalities, identified by fluorescence in situ hybridization during screening and the Revised International Staging System (R-ISS) score was determined based on ISS stage (based on serum β2-microglobulin and albumin levels), the presence of t(4; 14) or del(17p) chromosomal abnormalities, and baseline serum lactate dehydrogenase. The trial was registered at www.ClinicalTrials.gov (identifier: NCT02541383) and all patients provided written informed consent. The study protocol was approved by a local independent ethics committee or institutional review board at each study site.

sec.title: [18F]FDG-PET/CT acquisition and analysis
sec.p: [18F]FDG-PET/CT scans were performed at baseline (prior to the initiation of the induction treatment) in each center. All patients fasted for at least 6 hours prior to undergoing [18F]FDG-PET/CT scan. Dexamethasone was not to be administered within 12 hours before the [18F]FDG-PET/CT scan. Blood glucose levels were measured before the injection of [18F]FDG with a target glycemia level ≤150 mg/dL; however levels up to 200 mg/dL were allowed. No insulin was administered within 2 hours before the injection of [18F]FDG, and no oral contrast medium was given. Patients could receive a mild oral sedative before the [18F]FDG injection if required. Whole-body imaging (from the top of the head to the feet, with arms along the body) was performed 55 to 75 minutes after the [18F]FDG injection. The acquired imaging data were uploaded to a central electronic repository system (Keosys, Saint-Herblain, France).

The conventional PET-derived biomarkers that were assessed included the following visual and semi-quantitative parameters: the Deauville score for BM, classified as either 1 to 3 or 4 to 5; the presence of EMD and/or PMD; the BM SUVmax, measured using a 4 cm3 region of interest placed inside the L4 or L5 vertebral body and excluding FL; the SUVmax, defined as the highest SUVmax among all abnormalities (BM, FL, EMD, and PMD) and the total number of FLs, identified according to IMPeTUs criteria.22 A FL was defined as foci >5 mm with an intensity greater than that of normal BM background, and present on at least 2 consecutive slices. All benign related diseases were excluded. Diffuse BMI was defined as homogeneous or heterogeneous uptake in the axial and appendicular skeleton that was higher than liver uptake (ie, Deauville score of 4 or 5). EMD was defined as soft tissue invasion without contiguous bone involvement and PMD as soft tissue invasion with contiguous bone involvement. Therefore, PET positivity was defined as the presence of at least 1 FL or EMD or PMD, or diffuse BMI.11

Experienced physicians first manually delineated the FLs, then segmentation was performed using a previously described majority voting approach23 to derive TMTV-FL (including EMD, if present). This resulted in the final lesion identification required for calculating TMTV-FL. The mTMTV was then extracted automatically using the approach described in the supplemental Data. In this context, the median liver SUV, one of the thresholds proposed in the seminal study by Sachpekidis et al,17 was used to define pathological [18F]FDG uptake of FLs and diffuse BMI when present. Consequently, mTMTV encompassed both the FLs and diffuse BMI values at or above the predefined threshold.

sec.title: End points and statistical analyses
sec.p: The primary endpoints were PFS and OS. The clinical end point of PFS was defined as the time from first randomization until either disease progression according to International Myeloma Working Group’s criteria or death from any cause. OS was defined as the time from first randomization until death from any cause. Categorical variables were reported as counts and percentages, whereas continuous variables were presented as medians with interquartile ranges. The clinical and biological features considered were age, sex, the R-ISS score, high-risk cytogenetic abnormalities (presence of t[4;14] or del[17p]), and hemoglobin.

Firstly, the following conventional regression approaches were used to model time-to-event survival data. A receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve was constructed and the optimal cutoff point was identified by maximizing the Youden index. Corresponding survival curves were then generated at the univariate level using the Kaplan-Meier method based on this cutoff point. Univariate Cox analysis was performed to estimate the association between each feature and survival. Because the Cox model requires a sufficient number of events per predictor to prevent overfitting,24 only features with significant P values and a minimum of 10 events per feature were included in the subsequent multivariate Cox analysis. The stability of the extracted features was also evaluated using a LASSO-based Cox regression model (supplemental Data). A P value of < .05 was considered statistically significant.

Secondly, to overcome the limitations of conventional survival analysis, which typically rely on linear assumptions and proportional hazards, an advanced machine learning (ML) pipeline was implemented based on an ensemble learning model. The full original data set was divided into training and test sets using stratified random sampling, with respective proportions of 67% and 33%. The following steps were first fitted on the training set and subsequently applied to the test set to predict PFS and OS outcomes. Zero variance features were removed from the extracted features and the remaining features underwent Z-score normalization. The most informative features were selected through 500 bootstrap samples using the concordance index (C-index) for feature ranking, with the overall rank computed based on the importance score.25 Time-to-event survival data were modeled using 4 base estimators, including Cox proportional hazards, support vector machines, gradient boosting with component-wise least squares as the base learner, and random survival forests. A stratified nested cross-validation strategy comprising 3 outer and 3 inner folds was employed (supplemental Figure 1). The model’s hyperparameters (supplemental Table 1) and the number of selected features were optimized using Bayesian search over 300 iterations to maximize the C-index. Finally, the predicted risk scores were averaged from the 4 optimized ML models within each outer fold to calculate the final risk scores for the outer test samples using an ensemble technique. Feature importance was assessed using Shapley Additive Explanations values. Model performance on the test set was evaluated using the C-index. The final result was obtained from the outer fold test set and summarized as mean values. All analyses were conducted using R software, version 4.5.1, and Python, version 3.8.

sec.title: Patients
sec.p: Of the 274 patients in the CASSIOPET study who underwent a baseline [18F]FDG-PET/CT scan, 195 patients were treated with DARA. Following a median follow-up period of 80.1 months (interquartile range, 75.7-85.6), 91 progressions were observed and 33 deaths were recorded. The corresponding clinical/biological and PET-derived characteristics are summarized in Table 1. Of these patients, only 187 (95.9%) had both clinical and PET-derived features available for evaluation with ML models.

sec.title: Univariate and multivariate analyses
sec.p: Table 2 shows the results of the univariate analysis evaluating the prognostic value of all extracted features for PFS and OS. For PFS, the most significant PET-derived adverse prognostic factors were increased mTMTV (hazard ratio [HR], 1.07; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.03-1.11; P < .001), increased BM SUVmax (HR, 1.19; 95%CI, 1.08-1.33; P < .001), and PET positivity (HR, 2.06; 95% CI, 1.10-3.87; P = .02; Figure 2C). The optimal cut-offs for stratifying the DARA population into high- and low-risk groups, as determined by ROC curves, were 547 cm3 (P < .001; Figure 2A) for mTMTV, and 2.25 (P = .008; Figure 2B) for BM SUVmax. Of the clinical and biological features examined, anemia (HR, 1.14; 95% CI, 1.04-1.25; P = .005) and R-ISS score (HR, 1.93; 95% CI, 1.31-2.85; P < .001; Figure 6A) were identified as the most significant adverse prognostic factors for PFS. High-risk cytogenetic abnormalities with presence of Del[17p] and/or t[4;14] were identified as a moderate adverse prognostic factor (HR, 1.62; 95% CI, 0.98-2.69; P = .061). Multivariate analysis revealed that high mTMTV values (HR, 1.08; 95% CI, 1.03-1.12; P < .001) and R-ISS scores (HR, 1.73; 95% CI, 1.16-2.60; P = .008) were independent adverse prognostic factors. An additional analysis in which the R-ISS score was replaced by cytogenetic risk did not alter the results, with high mTMTV values (HR, 1.08; 95% CI, 1.04-1.12; P < .001) and high-risk cytogenetic abnormalities (HR, 1.78; 95% CI, 1.05-2.99; P = .032) remaining independent adverse prognostic factors. The LASSO-based Cox regression model identified mTMTV as the only stable feature (supplemental Figure 2A).

sec.p: Regarding OS, a greater number of PET-derived features were associated with a poor prognosis by univariate analysis. These included mTMTV (HR, 1.11; 95% CI, 1.05-1.16; P < .001), BM SUVmax (HR, 1.33; 95% CI, 1.15-1.53; P < .001), SUVmax (HR, 1.04; 95% CI, 1.00-1.08; P = .02), and the presence of PMD (HR, 2.35; 95% CI, 1.14-4.86; P = .02; Figure 3D). The optimal cutoffs were 515 cm3 (P < .001; Figure 3A) for mTMTV, 4.44 (P = .002; Figure 3B) for BM SUVmax and 4.26 (P = .03; Figure 3C) for SUVmax. As with the PFS analysis, anemia (HR, 1.2; 95% CI, 1.03-1.41; P = .02) and high R-ISS score (HR, 4.07; 95% CI, 2.13-7.80; P < .001; Figure 6C) were identified as the most significant adverse factors for OS, alongside with high-risk cytogenetic abnormalities (HR, 2.95; 95% CI, 1.43-6.09; P = .003). In the same way as the PFS analysis, multivariate analysis revealed that only high mTMTV values (HR, 1.10; 95% CI, 1.05-1.16; P < .001) and R-ISS scores (HR, 3.76; 95% CI, 1.91-7.38; P < .001) were independent adverse prognostic factors. The additional analysis considering high-risk cytogenetic abnormalities rather than R-ISS scores did not alter the identification of high mTMTV values (HR, 1.11; 95% CI, 1.06-1.17; P < .001) and high-risk cytogenetic abnormalities (HR, 3.69; 95% CI, 1.77-7.72; P < .001) as independent adverse prognostic factors. The LASSO-based Cox regression model identified R-ISS as the only stable feature (supplemental Figure 2B). Neither TMTV-FL nor EMD were associated with PFS (P = .21 and P = .14, respectively) or OS (P = .11 and P = .32, respectively) in the univariate analysis.

sec.title: ML analysis
sec.p: Incorporating all available PET-derived features and clinical prognostic biomarkers into an ensemble model yielded a C-index of 0.609 (range, 0.580-0.631) for PFS prediction. mTMTV was found to be the most informative feature, accounting for 25.6% of the model’s performance (Figure 4A). In combination with R-ISS and BM SUVmax, these features accounted over 50% of the model’s predictive importance. For OS prediction, the ensemble model achieved a C-index of 0.659 (range, 0.563-0.725), with mTMTV ranked first in importance, contributing 20.7%. Combined with total number of FLs and R-ISS, these 3 features collectively provided over 50% of the model’s predictive power (Figure 4B). Kaplan-Meier curves for the ensemble model, obtained from the outer folds over the test set using the cut-off point determined by the ROC curve of the training set, are shown in supplemental Figures 3 and 4.

sec.p: Figure 5 illustrates the influence of mTMTV on model prediction, showing automated mTMTV extraction for 2 patients. Figure 5A shows a low-risk patient with an mTMTV value of 96.4 cm3 and an R-ISS stage II, who did not experience death or disease progression. Figure 5B shows a high-risk patient with an mTMTV value of 1007.4 cm3 and an R-ISS stage II, who experienced disease progression 33 months after the start of therapy and died at 61 months.

caption.p: Representative patients with low- and high-risk mTMTV involvement. A low-risk 65-year-old female with mTMTV of 96.4 cm3 and R-ISS stage II (A), and a high-risk 60-year-old male with mTMTV of 1007.4 cm3 and R-ISS stage II (B). Both patients received bortezomib, thalidomide, and dexamethasone in the first randomization phase and DARA in the second.

sec.p: Due to their complementary nature, R-ISS and mTMTV were combined to identify high-risk patients, with a particular focus on those in R-ISS stage II, as this category accounts for the largest proportion of patients (133/195; 68%) with potentially heterogeneous outcomes. To this end, and because the mTMTV thresholds identified for PFS and OS were similar, we used the mTMTV threshold identified for PFS to analyze OS. This enabled to create 2 new patient subgroups that initially behaved as R-ISS stage II (Figure 6B,D). Patients in the subgroup with R-ISS stage II and high mTMTV had similar outcomes to those with R-ISS stage III, with a 5-year PFS of 43% (compared to 42% for R-ISS stage III). Patients with low mTMTV and R-ISS stage II defined a new category with a 5-year PFS of 63%, which was slightly >54% observed for R-ISS stage II patients. For OS, the combination of mTMTV and R-ISS allowed a new intermediate subgroup to be identified. This subgroup encompasses patients with high mTMTV and R-ISS stage II with a 5-year OS of 81%. Meanwhile, patients with low mTMTV and R-ISS stage II had a similar 5-year OS to those with R-ISS stage I (92% vs 97%).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: The recent introduction of DARA, an anti-CD38 monoclonal antibody, in the frontline therapy of MM was a groundbreaking development in the management of this disease, significantly improving patient outcomes. However, identifying patients with high-risk MM remains of major importance at the initial workup before anti-CD38 monoclonal antibody–based therapy. This study is the first to assess the prognostic value of [18F]FDG-PET/CT–derived mTMTV for PFS and OS in comparison with conventional PET biomarkers and the usual biological and chromosomal abnormalities in a large, prospective, homogeneous cohort of patients with NDMM who were treated with DARA for induction, consolidation or maintenance therapy, with long-term follow-up.

A high mTMTV value was a strong adverse prognostic factor independently associated with poorer PFS and OS. Interestingly, mTMTV emerged as the PET-derived biomarker with the greatest prognostic relevance. It outperformed all other conventional PET biomarkers and complemented R-ISS. This result confirms the relevance of the CT-based automated image segmentation approach previously proposed17 in a small cohort of patients with NDMM, now validated in a larger and more homogeneous cohort of patients with NDMM treated with DARA. One of the main advantages of the automated mTMTV computation is to eliminate the bias associated with manual segmentation and improves the reproducibility of the approach.

These results are concordant with other previously published works. Indeed, high TMTV values in the initial workup of patients with NDMM have been identified as independent adverse prognostic factors for PFS and OS in large cohorts of patients enrolled in Total Therapy 3A,13 as well as in another retrospective study,14 despite the fact that different segmentation techniques were used in these studies, resulting in differences in the TMTV prognostic cutoff values. Similar observations have also been reported in additional small, mixed, heterogeneous retrospective studies.15,16 However, it is important to note that these studies considered only the TMTV extracted from FLs (referred to as TMTV-FL in this work), which excludes diffuse BMI to some extent when present. The mTMTV assessed in this study encompasses both FLs and diffuse BMI with high [18F]FDG avidity (ie, higher than background liver uptake), reflecting the global medullary active metabolic tumor burden. This highlights the importance of incorporating diffuse BMI, if present, as this takes into account the less differentiated component of medullary infiltration, in addition to FL, which is known to affect prognosis. According to conventional survival analysis, TMTV-FL had no significant impact in our study. This finding is further reinforced by the ML-based results, which revealed that the contribution of TMTV-FL was small in comparison with that of other parameters for both PFS and OS.

A high BM SUVmax value was another strong PET-based adverse prognostic factor for PFS and OS by univariate analysis, as previously demonstrated.10 This biomarker has been suggested as a surrogate for clonal plasma cell differentiation,26 and high BM SUVmax values reflecting low clonal plasma cell differentiation seem to be of prognostic relevance in NDMM. The optimal BM SUVmax cutoff values distinguishing the risk groups were 2.25 for predicting PFS and 4.44 for OS prediction. Baseline PET positivity was also of pejorative prognostic significance for PFS only by univariate analysis. This result is consistent with a previous interim analysis of CASSIOPET,11 in which the follow-up period was shorter and the number of events was lower. Unlike the previous report,11 the presence of EMD did not significantly predict adverse PFS or OS in this analysis mainly because the follow-up period was longer than in the previous study.

One of the strengths of this study is that conventional survival analyses were validated using ML statistical analysis. Interestingly, the ML approach revealed that numerous PET-derived parameters were prognostic factors for both PFS and OS in the era of anti-CD38 monoclonal antibody as a frontline therapy, including mTMTV, BM SUVmax, SUVmax, Deauville score for BM, PMD and the number of FLs. This approach has the advantage of addressing the limitations of conventional survival models by capturing complex nonlinear interactions among all extracted features. Additionally, an ensemble ML strategy was employed where time-to-event survival data were modeled using 4 ML algorithms within a nested cross-validation technique. Integrating both linear and nonlinear models gives this ensemble model the ability to make more reliable risk predictions and provide a more robust assessment of feature importance. Finally, this added analysis strengthened the conventional analysis by identifying the top 10 most significant prognostic biomarkers with the greatest impact on model performance (Figure 4).

As expected, the high R-ISS score predicted shorter PFS and OS independently.27 We acknowledge that only high-risk chromosomal abnormalities [deletion(17p) and translocations t(4;14)(p16;q32) or t(14;16)(q32;q23)] were considered in the calculation of the R-ISS score, and that new high-risk abnormalities1 such as TP53 mutations, 1q+ and/or del(1p32), and monoallelic del(1p32) alongside 1q+ or biallelic del(1p32) were unavailable in this cohort. Univariate analysis revealed that the presence of anemia at baseline was also a negative prognostic factor for both PFS and OS, which is consistent with our previously reported results for a different combination of NDMM prospective cohorts.10

This study highlights the complementary nature of functional imaging and BM cytological assessment in predicting the prognosis stratification in MM. Indeed, Rasche et al28,29 have demonstrated that high-risk genomic alterations can be present in large FLs seen on PET scans but absent in other locations. They also demonstrated that intra-patient spatial genomic heterogeneity can limit the sensitivity of risk classification based solely on cytogenetics and gene expression profiling due to the sampling effect. However, in this study, the complementary nature of PET-derived mTMTV and BM cytological assessment is subject to the absence of new high-risk cytogenetic abnormalities1 assessed.

Finally, a combination of R-ISS and [18F]FDG-PET–based information has been proposed to more effectively stratify patients. Indeed, in the era of new therapies, too many patients are classified as R-ISS stage II. By incorporating PET data, as proposed in lymphoma,30 we can reclassify patients and improve risk stratification. Three new categories could be introduced for PFS: R-ISS stage I, low mTMTV/R-ISS stage II, and the combination of R-ISS stage III with high mTMTV/R-ISS stage II. Similarly, 3 new categories could be introduced for OS: the combination of R-ISS stage I with low mTMTV/R-ISS stage II, high TMTV/R-ISS stage II, and R-ISS stage III. This suggests that metabolic information could be used alongside R-ISS score to improve risk classification.

From a practical standpoint, the computation of mTMTV is straightforward once automated bone and liver segmentation tools are available. The method only requires standard [18F]FDG-PET/CT data sets and uses the median liver SUV as a patient-specific reference, allowing harmonized thresholding across scanners and centers. After segmentation, mTMTV is automatically derived without manual contouring, which substantially reduces inter-observer variability compared with lesion-based TMTV approaches. As artificial intelligence–based and vendor-neutral segmentation tools become more widely available, mTMTV quantification could easily be incorporated into clinical or research workflows to support risk stratification at baseline in patients with NDMM.

In conclusion, this prospective study confirmed the prognostic relevance of [18F]FDG-PET/CT–based parameters in the initial workup of patients with NDMM in the era of anti-CD38 monoclonal antibody–based therapy. An increased [18F]FDG-PET/CT–derived mTMTV value was reported as a strong and independent adverse prognostic biomarker for PFS and OS, regardless of R-ISS. This could be proposed as a new high-risk biomarker in the initial workup of patients with NDMM. An ML-based survival model confirmed this finding, as well as the contribution of several other PET-based parameters to prognostic determination, such as BM SUVmax. A new scoring system combining the R-ISS score and the [18F]FDG-PET-based mTMTV value could be proposed to stratify patients more accurately. However, this needs to be confirmed in other large cohorts of patients with NDMM in which high-risk cytogenetic abnormalities have been assessed, such as in the upcoming ancillary MIDAS PET study.
